newsitem.title: USA: Glickman says CRP guidelines to be released soon.
newsitem.headline: Glickman says CRP guidelines to be released soon.

text.p: Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Wednesday that the USDA is "about to release" the government's new guidelines for the Conservation Reserve Program, and that enrollment is expected to begin by March.

Speaking at the National Press Club, Glickman said the focus of the program will be to enroll the most fragile land in the CRP and to bring back to production "less erodible land better suited for planting crops."
He said he would not approve cutting CRP funds in order to fund other budget programs. "We aren't going to take its (CRP) money and use it for other programs," Glickman said.
Glickman stressed the need to increase the safety net for farmers under the farm bill passed last year by Congress.

He said that although he sees stronger U.S. crop prices over the next decade, he also predicts more volatility and bigger swings in prices. He said the current safety net under the new farm bill is insufficient if prices drop sharply.
"We don't have a sufficient safety net for farmers if prices drop sharply ... we do if they stay at current levels," Glickman said in response to questions.

Glickman said the Clinton administration's budget will include proposals to help provide farmers with better markets for their crops and to deal with fluctuating prices. "There will be a section dealing with safety net issues," he said.
Asked how large a grain reserve USDA would seek if it sends such a proposal to Congress, Glickman said the department has not yet made a final decision on re-establishing a reserve.
"At this stage we haven't made the decision about whether in fact to send such a proposal to Congress," Glickman said. "We have no specific grain reserve proposal ready to go."
Glickman also said he would not support efforts to end tax incentives for corn-based ethanol, and said the marketplace would determine future demand for ethanol.

The Agriculture Secretary reiterated his expectations that there will be no major changes in the recently passed farm bill this year. He said that rather than increasing loan rates to strengthen the so-called safety net for farmers, which he speculated Congress would not pass this year, he would look at the option of possibly extending the time farmers have to pay back crop loans.
